position: Gibbon’s photographs show the feet closing, the arms rising overhead and the hands returning low.
attention: Watch the relationship between the closing step and the start of the arm circle.

position: Gibbon shows an advance, withdrawal and quarter-turn, with rounded forearm actions.
attention: Compare the palms in the photograph manual with Ewers’s description; keep each teacher’s version intact.
application: Ewers reads the sequence through ward-off, yielding, squeezing and pressing. This is his later teaching interpretation.

position: Gibbon’s plates alternate forward and rear-weighted positions as the hands circle.
attention: Follow one full cycle of returning and advancing before comparing the next cycle.
application: Ewers describes linked receiving and forward palm actions. His account does not establish a single compulsory fighting application.

position: Gibbon includes wide standing, side weighting, feet together and overhead arm positions in this six-movement passage.
attention: Notice that this named sequence contains several different shapes; a single crane photograph cannot represent it all.
application: Ewers identifies a body-bumping possibility in the folding and weight transfer of his Crane sequence.

position: Gibbon labels the three photographed phases Dragon, Duck and Dragon.
attention: Keep the change of supporting leg visible when reading the turning hands.
application: Ewers interprets the advance–retreat–advance through receiving, turning and returning force. His partner example is a later interpretation, not a recovered instruction from a Chee Soo plate.

position: Ewers describes drawing the right fist beneath the opposite elbow while withdrawing, then stepping right and opening the right arm across the body.
attention: Follow the fist and the supporting elbow separately, then consider how they travel together.
application: Ewers discusses grasping in relation to this named posture in his later account of the plucking method.

position: Ewers emphasises the shared timing of both hands and the waist-led sideways sweep. He criticises versions in which one hand becomes still.
attention: Watch the less prominent hand as closely as the hand passing the knee.
application: A name shared with Yang practice does not identify the same application. Compare the Lee lesson’s actual hand path before proposing a partner exercise.

position: Ewers uses Repulse the Monkey to illustrate rotation of the waist while the hips remain facing forward in his version.
attention: Distinguish a change of the shoulders from a change in the direction of the feet.

position: Ewers describes four actions: the first two on one leg, then a return to ground contact and a forward step. The raised foot extends before returning.
attention: Look for the moment of renewed heel contact rather than judging balance from the raised-leg photograph alone.
application: Ewers assigns receiving, ward-off and other force relationships to both the arms and the lifted leg. This is an interpretation of the whole moving sequence.

position: Ewers records a version with upright palms and contrasts it with a later version with palms facing down. His chronology is personal testimony.
attention: Record palm direction and stance together when comparing demonstrations.
application: His later Double Whip article discusses several force methods within the sequence; its name does not prescribe one isolated strike.

position: The named lesson covers movements 33–36. Ewers also discusses a Large Snake Unwinds posture, but an exact equivalence with this numbered Cobra passage has not been established here.
attention: Use the numbered lesson to identify the turn and exit; do not substitute a similarly named snake posture.

position: The named video lesson covers movements 37–40. A sufficiently detailed written account of these four phases has not been verified in the sources reviewed.
attention: In the lesson, trace the supporting foot through the passage and record each change of facing before comparing any still image.

position: The named video lesson covers movements 41–44. The peacock name alone does not establish the hand shape, stance or martial use.
attention: Observe the order in which the arms open and return; avoid selecting a still simply because its silhouette suggests a tail.

position: This second Brush Knee passage occupies movements 45–46. Ewers’s general discussion of the posture stresses that both hands continue to move together.
attention: Compare its entry with set 7 before assuming the repeated name means an identical transition.

position: This passage ends the first 50 movements. Ewers’s separate Cyclone practice stresses continuous circular movement and coordination of legs, torso, arms, breath and attention.
attention: Watch the exit from movement 50 as well as the circular arm action; the complete form continues beyond this teaching division.

position: The linked lesson identifies Single Whip Unleashed as movements 51–52. A phase-by-phase written description has not been verified here.
attention: Compare the entry from Edge of the Cyclone with the exit into Double Whip; avoid importing the Yang Single Whip shape.

position: Wood describes gathering towards the body followed by an outward, rounded expansion.
attention: Compare this return of Double Whip with set 10 without assuming the entry direction is the same.

position: Wood describes a sweep towards the east followed by movement to the right, forward, upward and downward.
attention: Distinguish the overall direction of travel from the smaller rise and fall of the hands.

position: Wood’s outline moves from gathering inward to a chopping action, another collection and a closing action.
attention: Follow the sequence of gathering and releasing; the animal name is a memory aid, not evidence of origin.

position: Wood’s short description identifies a step left and an aiming action.
attention: Use the lesson to establish which hand leads. An archer name does not determine left and right on its own.

position: Wood describes turning right, then left, followed by a drawing-in action through the imagery of controlling a horse.
attention: Follow the reversals of direction through the feet as well as the hands.

position: Wood outlines a rightward sweep followed by a return to the left, using the whip image for the action.
attention: Distinguish this three-movement passage from Single Whip Unleashed at set 16.

position: Wood describes a rightward sweep and inward return, followed by an outward action to the right and then the left.
attention: Compare this longer return of Repulse the Monkey with the two-movement passage at set 8.

position: Wood describes an encircling action linking east and west. Her public outline does not specify each foot placement.
attention: Treat the directional language as a cue to examine the demonstration, not a complete stepping diagram.

position: Wood describes opposing downward and upward actions, followed by a warding action with the right arm and raised right leg.
attention: Watch how the upper and lower limbs exchange roles when the leg rises.

position: Wood outlines a leftward roll, a backward step and rightward draw, then an extension and cutting action.
attention: Follow the backward step before considering the final reach; an endpoint photograph would omit that preparation.

position: The linked lesson covers movements 83–87. Wood’s public listing confirms the title but supplies no movement description.
attention: Identify the five numbered phases in the lesson. No organ, element or breathing correspondence is assigned here without a specific source.

position: Wood describes turning towards the south and then the east in this return of Double Whip.
attention: Compare the direction changes with the earlier Double Whip passages; repeated titles retain separate entries.

position: Wood’s outline includes a kick with opposing warding actions, a backward step, a forward action and a return to the centre.
attention: This Lee passage includes actions not implied by the familiar Cloud Hands name. Follow the linked Lee lesson rather than substituting a Yang pattern.

position: Wood describes clearing to the right and front, sweeping right, covering the front and withdrawing.
attention: Track the relationship between the sweep and the retreat; avoid fixing the meaning of the wind image to one technique.

position: Wood describes a step right, a turn forward, a right kick, and a step and turn left.
attention: Follow the sequence of facing changes before studying the animal imagery.

position: Wood outlines a draw towards the centre, a right turn and downward press, followed by a lift outward to the right.
attention: Notice the change from lowering to lifting. The scissors image does not itself establish a joint lock.

position: Wood describes turning into a mounted stance, drawing inward and expanding towards an intended direction.
attention: Compare this release with the preparation imagery at set 20, while keeping their different places in the form clear.

position: Wood describes an inward and downward action followed by a backward step and an action to the right.
attention: Compare this third Brush Knee entry with sets 7 and 14; note what the previous sequence changes.

position: Wood outlines a right turn and lift, a circle and downward press, then a left sweep, downward chop and rightward backhand action.
attention: Follow the reversals through the middle of the passage, not just the larger circles suggested by the title.

position: Wood describes a left turn and repeated drawing-in actions using the image of restraining and mounting a wild horse.
attention: Compare the drawing actions with Mount the Wild Horse at set 21 without treating the two passages as interchangeable.

position: Wood’s outline begins with a backward step and inward draw, followed by pushing away and leftward warding with opposing actions.
attention: Separate this Playful Monkey passage from the earlier Repulse the Monkey sequences.

position: Wood describes left and right warding, a lift and kick, then a right turn and outward expansion.
attention: Watch the preparation for the kick before following the turn; do not infer a high kick from the title.

position: Wood’s outline alternates stepping, turns, drawing inward, outward actions and a rising sweep across this eight-movement passage.
attention: This is a named part of the Lee main form. It is not identified here with an independent Eight Brocades qigong routine.

position: Wood describes drawing back and inward with a right turn, then lowering, expanding forward and returning towards the chest.
attention: Treat inner-orbit language as traditional imagery. The catalogue does not prescribe an internal circulation exercise.

position: Wood describes a downward-to-upward expansion, opening to the sides and folding back inward.
attention: Compare the closing gathering with the opening set. The available video groups this passage and Finish within movements 138–140.

position: Wood identifies Finish as its own set and describes relaxing after completing the long hand form.
attention: Allow the ending to remain part of the sequence. The precise numbered boundary between sets 41 and 42 is unresolved in the checked sources.
